genZNote: Mold in the soil, spherule full of endospores in your lungs — and the mold form is dangerous enough in a lab that it needs BSL-3 handling.

morphology.shape: Dimorphic: septate hyphae with arthroconidia in soil/culture (25-30°C); large spherules containing endospores in tissue (37°C)
morphology.size: Arthroconidia ~2-4 x 3-6 µm; spherules can reach 20-100 µm, packed with endospores

habitat.naturalHabitat: Soil of arid and semi-arid regions, particularly the southwestern United States (California's San Joaquin Valley, Arizona) and parts of Mexico and Central/South America
habitat.hostAssociation: Not host-associated in its mold/environmental form; infects humans and animals via inhalation
habitat.environmentalOccurrence: Arthroconidia become airborne when contaminated soil is disturbed (construction, dust storms, farming, earthquakes)

microscopy.stain: KOH prep or histopathology of tissue/sputum
microscopy.appearance: Large, thick-walled spherules containing endospores in tissue; septate hyphae with barrel-shaped arthroconidia in mold-phase culture
microscopy.arrangement: Spherules in tissue; arthroconidia chains in mold culture

culture.media: Sabouraud dextrose agar; mold-phase cultures pose a significant laboratory hazard
culture.growthCharacteristics: Dimorphic — mold at 25-30°C, spherule/tissue form at 37°C in vivo; mold-phase cultures must be handled under BSL-3 containment due to highly infectious airborne arthroconidia
culture.colonyMorphology: White to gray, cottony mold colonies

biochemicalTests.result: Reflects prior exposure/immunity (not used for acute diagnosis)

identificationClues: Endemic exposure history — travel to or residence in the southwestern US (California, Arizona) or endemic areas of Mexico/Central-South America
Large spherules packed with endospores seen on histopathology of infected tissue
Mold-phase cultures are highly infectious via inhalation of arthroconidia — the lab must be alerted before processing suspected specimens (BSL-3 handling)
Serologic testing (complement fixation, immunodiffusion) is the primary diagnostic approach; the organism should not be handled/cultured outside appropriate containment

diseases: Coccidioidomycosis ('Valley Fever') — primary pulmonary infection, often subclinical or self-limited flu-like illness; can cause community-acquired pneumonia
Disseminated disease (skin, bone, joint, meningitis) in a minority of cases, more common in immunocompromised patients, pregnant women, and certain ethnic groups with higher susceptibility
virulenceFactors: Spherule formation in tissue — evades phagocytosis and releases hundreds of endospores upon rupture, each capable of forming a new spherule
Thick spherule wall resisting host immune clearance
clinicalImportance.transmission: Inhalation of airborne arthroconidia from disturbed soil (construction, farming, wind/dust storms, earthquakes); not transmitted person-to-person
clinicalImportance.epidemiology: Endemic to the arid southwestern United States, especially California's San Joaquin Valley and Arizona, as well as parts of Mexico and Central/South America; incidence rises after soil disturbance events and periods of drought followed by rain
clinicalImportance.labSignificance: Laboratory staff must be notified in advance when Coccidioides is suspected — the mold-phase culture is highly infectious via inhalation and requires BSL-3 containment for safe handling

examFacts.shape: Dimorphic — mold with arthroconidia; spherules with endospores in tissue
examFacts.importantTest: Serology (complement fixation/immunodiffusion); histopathology showing spherules; mold culture requires BSL-3
examFacts.distinguishingFeature: A dimorphic desert fungus forming spherules packed with endospores in tissue — its mold-phase culture is dangerously infectious and requires BSL-3 handling
